repo_notes.content:
WHAT THIS PROJECT IS. MiSTer Tasty plays published tool-assisted (TAS) movies back on real MiSTer FPGA cores. The command-line tool is `tasty`. It runs on the ARM side of a DE10-Nano (the Cyclone V HPS), loads the core and the user's own ROM, and writes each controller input to the core on the frame the movie asks for. Nothing is attached to the controller port and no extra hardware is needed. People use it to watch a run on real gateware, and core developers use it to find the first frame where a core's picture differs from the emulator a movie was recorded on.

Around the tool the repository ships: an installer (`install.sh`), a one-line try-it wrapper (`test-tasty.sh`), a MiSTer Scripts-menu entry (`scripts/Tasty.sh`), a catalogue of runs (`data/tas-catalog.tsv`), a desktop comparison tool (`tools/compare`, command `tasty-compare`), the recipe for a fully static armhf binary (`src/tools/`, `cmake/arm-linux-gnueabihf-static.cmake`), tests (`tests/`) and GitHub Actions workflows (`.github/workflows/`).

SCOPE TO KEEP ON EVERY PAGE. Tasty borrows the FPGA for one run: `tasty play` stops the MiSTer binary that is running, shows a short splash, loads the core, plays the movie, and starts `/media/fat/MiSTer` again when the run is over (30 seconds after the last input unless `--linger`, `--stay` or `tasty stop` says otherwise). Describe it as a replay tool that hands the machine back, never as a general MiSTer front end or a substitute for the stock MiSTer binary. It never downloads a ROM, never opens the user's own save files, and changes core settings only in memory for the run. It is an independent community project, not affiliated with the MiSTer FPGA project.

STATUS. The project is early. Take the version, the per-system status (NES works; SNES works for some movies; Genesis / Mega Drive is experimental; PlayStation does not stay in sync yet) and the tables of known-good, candidate and desyncing runs from `README.md` only. Do not derive a list of supported systems from the number of core classes in the source: the tree carries support classes for many more cores than the four systems Tasty has movie codecs for.

AUTHORITATIVE SOURCES, in this order.

1. `README.md`: what the tool does, its status, the tables of runs, `--lead`, what a movie needs, the command line, recording, the recommended kernel settings, and the build steps.
2. `tools/compare/README.md`: `tasty-compare`, its dependencies, the columns of the `*.frames.tsv` sidecar, and the emulator dump recipes.
3. The usage text and the option table in `src/firmware/tasty_cli.cpp`, with `TastyArgs` and `TastyVerb` in `tasty_cli.h`, `TastyRefusal` in `tasty_cli_refusal.h` and the sentences in `tasty_sentences.cpp`: the exact command grammar and every refusal message.
4. The comment blocks at the top of `install.sh`, `test-tasty.sh`, `scripts/Tasty.sh`, `data/tas-catalog.tsv`, `tests/menu/run.sh`, `tests/install/run.sh`, `tests/try/run.sh` and the two workflow files: these say what each script does and which environment variables exist for testing.
5. `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md` and `licenses/`: what the static binary links and under which terms.
6. `LICENSE`: the code is GPL-3.0-or-later.

HOW TO READ THE C++. The C++ and `.slint` sources carry no explanatory comments, only one SPDX line per file. Behaviour has to be read from type and function names, from `static_assert` messages (many state the rule they enforce in a sentence), from enum names, and from the strings the program prints. Prefer those to guesses. Quote file paths, type names and option names exactly as they appear; never invent a function, an option, a file or a figure. Where the code and the README seem to disagree about something a user can see, report both rather than choosing one.

NAMES. The CMake executable target is `mister_exe` and its output file is `MiSTer` (`build/<preset>/src/firmware/MiSTer`); the release copies and strips it as `tasty`. `src/firmware/main.cpp` runs the tasty command grammar when the program's file name contains `tasty`, or when the first argument is `tasty`. The namespace is `mister`, the library targets are `mister_*`, and build options and macros are `TASTY_*`. These are just names in this tree; write about the tool as `tasty`.

DIRECTORIES THAT MATTER MOST, most important first.

- `src/firmware/`: the executable. `main.cpp`; the tasty command: entry and grammar (`tasty_entry`, `tasty_cli`, `tasty_cli_refusal.h`), one class per verb (`tasty_command`), the short client (`tasty_client`), checks before a run (`tasty_preflight`, `tasty_movie`, `tasty_record`), the run's files (`tasty_paths`, `tasty_owner_lock`, `tasty_pid_file`, `tasty_status_file`), stopping and restarting the stock binary (`tasty_stock_control`, `tasty_home_lane`, `tasty_return_home.h`), the run itself (`tasty_session`, `tasty_splash`, `tasty_sink`, `replay_port.h`) and its messages (`tasty_sentences`, `tasty_say`, `tasty_writeback`); the session mode a run uses (`replay_mode`, behind the `SessionMode` interface in `session_mode.h`); process bring-up and shutdown (`process_standup`, `rt_setup`, `memory_policy_outcome`); thread creation and join order (`thread_assembly`); and the composition of the object graph (`hub`, `assembly.h`, `board_parts`, `device_block`, `replay_block`, `recorder_block`).
- `src/l4_app/`: the replay engine (`replay_feeder`, `scan_stage`, `hash_stage`, `settle_stage`, `run_stage`, `replay_play`, `replay_ring`, `replay_msg`, `replay_gate`, `epoch_rule.h`, `frame_reference.h`, `replay_status`), the real-time main (`rt_main`), the link session and its owner (`link_session`, `session_owner`), core loading (`core_switch`, `bitstream_programmer`, `load_*`), and the recorder (`frame_copier`, `frame_hasher`, `avi_*`, `cscd_codec`, `zmbv_codec`, `sidecar_writer`).
- `src/l3_cores/`: movie codecs (`movie_codec`, `movie_system`, `i_movie_format.h`, `i_replay_core.h`, `nes_*`, `snes_*`, `megadrive_*`, `psx_*` codec files), power-on RAM images (`ram_image*`), ROM digests (`rom_digest`), and the per-core classes, profiles and manifests.
- `src/l1_proto/`: the protocol spoken with a core. `src/l0_reactor/`: the real-time event loop. `src/l0_hal/`, `src/l0_boards/`, `src/l0_os/`: board description, FPGA access and Linux wrappers. `src/l2_services/`: files, config, input devices, video, storage and disc images. `src/infra/`: the cross-thread primitives and small utilities everything else uses. `src/l5_ui/`: on-screen menu pages.
- `scripts/Tasty.sh`, `install.sh`, `test-tasty.sh`, `data/tas-catalog.tsv`: what most users touch.
- `tools/compare/`: `tasty-compare` (Python) and the emulator dump scripts (Lua, plus a small .NET runner in `tricnes-dump/`). It runs on a desktop Linux PC, not on the DE10-Nano.
- `tests/`, `cmake/`, `CMakeLists.txt`, `CMakePresets.json`, `.github/workflows/`, `src/tools/`: build, test and release.

NOT SOURCE TO DOCUMENT AS CODE.
- `licenses/`: third-party licence texts, copied verbatim. Cite them; do not summarise them as project policy.
- `art/`: artwork (the mascot, banner, icons). Mention it in the overview and credits only.
- `src/l4_app/fonts/pixel-operator/`: third-party font files. `tools/compare/palettes/`: third-party NES palette data. `src/l4_app/assets/logo.png`: the front-end logo, decoded at build time by `src/tools/embed_logo.py`. `src/tools/slint/*.patch`: patches the build applies to the third-party Slint library.
- `build/`: build output, ignored by git.

THIRD-PARTY CODE IS FETCHED, NOT VENDORED. zlib-ng, lzo, minizip, libchdr and the Noto Sans fonts are downloaded and built by `src/tools/build-static-deps.py`, and the Slint UI library by `src/tools/build-static-slint.sh`, each at a pinned version and SHA-256. The host build uses the distribution's zlib, libchdr, minizip and lzo packages instead.

GENERATED AT BUILD TIME, not in the tree: `splash_embed.h` (made by `src/tools/embed_splash.py` from `art/banner.png`, see `src/firmware/CMakeLists.txt`) and the compiled HD menu header (made by the Slint compiler from `src/l4_app/slint/*.slint` when `TASTY_WITH_HDOSD` is on).

THE LAYER MODEL. The C++23 source under `src/` is eleven directories that form a strict stack. Each layer is one static library, its public headers live under `include/<prefix>/`, and it may include only from itself and the layers below it. The direction is fixed by `target_link_libraries(... PUBLIC ...)` in each layer's `CMakeLists.txt`. From the bottom up:

- `src/infra` (headers `infra/`, library `mister_infra`; namespaces `mister`, `mister::infra`, `mister::xthread`): depends on nothing in the tree. Errors (`Error`, `Ex<T>`), thread roles (`SeatTag`), the cross-thread primitives (`SpscRing`, `Telemetry`, `WakeFlag`, `LoanChannel`, `Inbox`), the thread main-loop template (`SeatMain`, `SeatPark`), message sum types (`message_sum.h`), fixed strings, parsing and statistics helpers.
- `src/l0_os` (`os/`, `mister_os`, `mister::os`): thin wrappers over Linux: clocks, memory mappings, evdev, uinput, the framebuffer device, I2C, UIO, scheduling, child processes, kernel probes.
- `src/l0_hal` (`hal/`, `mister_hal`, `mister::hal`): what a board is. `BoardProfile` and the boards table, register windows, the thread map, FPGA memory apertures, and the core link port (`ILinkPort`, `SpiBus`).
- `src/l0_reactor` (`reactor/`, `mister_reactor`) and `src/l0_boards` (`boards/`, `mister_boards`): both sit directly on `hal`. The reactor is the real-time event loop (`Executive`, `Notifier`, `LinkDecoderDecl`, `RoundTimer`, `FrameClock`). The boards layer holds each SoC family's bridge sequencing and FPGA programmer.
- `src/l1_proto` (`proto/`, `mister_proto`): sits on the reactor. The link protocol: opcodes, the config string, the status word, file transfer, block (disk) service, pad and keyboard encoders, the `LinkOp` / `LinkEvent` message types and the decoders.
- `src/l2_services` (`svc/`, `mister_services`): host services: `Vfs` and files, archives, config parsing, input devices and mapping, video timing and the HDMI transmitter, storage and disc images (cue/bin, CHD).
- `src/l3_cores` (`cores/`, `mister_cores`): per-core knowledge: the `Core` classes, `CoreProfile` manifests, the registry, loaders, CD engines, and the movie codecs.
- `src/l4_app` (`app/`, `mister_app`): the application: link session, session owner, core loading, the replay engine, input pipeline, video pump, recorder, and the HD menu renderer.
- `src/l5_ui` (`ui/`, `mister_ui`): on-screen menu pages, option items and the classic OSD renderer.
- `src/firmware` (namespace `mister::fw`): the top. Three libraries and the executable: `mister_fw_assembly` (links app, cores and boards), `mister_fw_tasty` (the tasty command; links the assembly only, not `mister_ui`), `mister_fw_menu` (links the assembly and `mister_ui`), and `mister_exe`.

RULES THAT HOLD ACROSS LAYERS. Upward includes do not exist: a lower layer learns about a higher one only through an interface it declares itself (for example `cores::IReplayCore`, `app::IOwnerTick`, `hal::ILinkPort`). The code is built with `-fno-exceptions` and `-fno-rtti`; fallible functions return `Ex<T>`, which is `std::expected<T, Error>`. Domain values are small named types rather than bare integers (`MovieFrame`, `FrameCount`, `ReplayLead`, `JoyMask`, `FileSize`, `CpuId`, ...). Tables are `constexpr` arrays checked by `static_assert`, so many facts in this tree are data rows, not branches. When describing a layer, name its directory and include prefix, and say which layers it may use.

THREADS. Every thread has one fixed role, called a seat, named by `SeatTag` in `src/infra/include/infra/seat.h`: T-RT, T-FRAME, T-INPUT, T-PCM, T-PREFETCH, T-DIAG, T-UI, T-IO, T-CAPTURE, T-ENCODE, T-RECWRITE, T-LAUNCHER, T-HDOSD, T-CONNECT, and MAIN (the process's first thread). Each seat's CPU, scheduling policy, priority and stack size is one row of a per-board table, `kDe10ThreadMap` in `src/l0_hal/include/hal/thread_map.h`. The `static_assert`s and `constexpr` predicates beside it state the invariants: T-RT holds the highest SCHED_FIFO priority, the FIFO seats are strictly ordered, and only T-RT and T-FRAME may sit on the real-time CPU. On the DE10-Nano that is CPU 1 (T-RT FIFO 40, T-FRAME FIFO 35); every other seat is on CPU 0 (T-INPUT 25, T-IO 23, T-PCM 22, T-CAPTURE 21, T-PREFETCH 20 under FIFO; T-DIAG, T-UI, T-ENCODE, T-RECWRITE, T-LAUNCHER, T-HDOSD and T-CONNECT under the default policy). T-CONNECT hosts the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth services of the MiSTer firmware; the code is carried in this tree and a `tasty` run never spawns it. Read the numbers from the table when writing; do not round or re-derive them.

HOW THE WORK IS DIVIDED.
- T-RT is the only thread that drives the core link. `app::RtMain` (`src/l4_app/src/rt_main.cpp`) runs one round each time `reactor::Executive` wakes it, on a 1 ms tick or an event. A round polls the link session, drains a bounded number of queued link operations from the other threads' channels, steps the replay gate (`app::ReplayGate`), the core frame counter, the scan-out relay and the disk lamp, lets the Executive service the registered link decoders, and spends what is left of a per-round word budget (`round_budget_words` in the board's timing row) on file-transfer words. It only moves prepared data between the core and the channels: it opens no files and decodes no movie.
- T-FRAME waits for vertical sync on the board's framebuffer device (`reactor::FrameClock`) and publishes a frame sequence number.
- T-UI runs the owner tick. In a Tasty run that is `fw::TastySession` (the run's stage machine) and `app::ReplayFeeder` (scan the movie, check the ROM digest, arm the gate, stream input records into the replay ring).
- T-IO does blocking storage work (mounted disk and disc images, save files); T-PREFETCH reads ahead in compressed disc images; T-PCM feeds PCM audio to cores that take it.
- T-INPUT reads Linux input devices and produces pad and keyboard operations for T-RT. While a replay is armed, T-RT drops live pad operations (`ReplayGate::suppresses`), so a stray press cannot change a run.
- T-CAPTURE copies the core's frames out of the scaler buffer, T-ENCODE hashes and compresses them, and T-RECWRITE writes the AVI and the per-frame hash log. The replay never waits for the recording.
- T-DIAG samples statistics and writes diagnostics. T-LAUNCHER and T-HDOSD belong to the menu code.
- MAIN brings the process up (`fw::ProcessStandup`), creates the seats (`fw::ThreadAssembly`), supervises, and shuts down.

HOW THREADS TALK. Threads do not share mutable objects and take no locks on the real-time path. A class is annotated with the seat that may call it: `TASTY_SEAT_RESIDENT(tag)` for one seat, `TASTY_SEAT_MEDIATOR(a, b)` for an object built to sit between two seats, `TASTY_SEAT_EXEMPT(kind)` for immutable shared data and boot-time code. Data crosses through a small set of primitives in `src/infra/include/infra/`: `SpscRing` (single-producer, single-consumer queue), `Telemetry` (a single-writer latest-value cell readers sample without blocking), `WakeFlag` (an eventfd-backed wake or stop flag) and `LoanChannel` (a pool whose slots one seat lends to another and gets back). Types such as `ReplayRing`, `LinkTxChannel`, `ReplayControlCell` and `ReplayStatusCell` are named compositions of those. When describing any flow, say which seat runs each step and which channel carries the hand-over.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE. Frame-exact replay depends on T-RT writing the pad state inside the right frame, every frame. A stall of more than one frame desyncs a run. That is why T-RT has a CPU nearly to itself, why memory is locked, and why the README recommends two `vm` sysctls and a writeback CPU mask.

ONE RUN, END TO END (use this as the spine for the pages on process lifecycle, frame timing and the command line; confirm each step in the named file).

1. `main` (`src/firmware/main.cpp`) calls `fw::tasty_invocation`, then `fw::run_tasty` (`tasty_entry.cpp`). `parse_tasty_args` turns argv into `TastyArgs`, and `make_tasty_command` (`tasty_command.cpp`) returns one `TastyCommand` object per verb. `info` and `check` run in the calling process and exit. `status`, `stop` and `rec stop` are clients (`fw::TastyClient`): they read `/tmp/tasty.status`, signal the process recorded in `/tmp/tasty.pid`, or send it a command line. `play` (and `rec start` when nothing is running) becomes the owner process.
2. The owner builds a `fw::ReplayMode` and hands it to `fw::ProcessStandup`. `ReplayMode::prepare` resolves paths, finds or checks the ROM (`TastyPreflight::play_rom`), takes `/tmp/tasty.lock` so only one run exists (`TastyOwnerLock`), stops the running MiSTer binary (`StockControl::stop`, through `HomeLane::stop_and_owe`), and records that it now owes a return to the menu. Signal handlers make sure `/media/fat/MiSTer` is started again even if the run is interrupted or crashes (`HomeLane::launch`).
3. `ProcessStandup::run` walks a fixed ladder: identify the board from the device tree, open the platform's register windows, check the FPGA is ready, open storage, assemble the object graph (`fw::Hub`), run the boot ladder, spawn the seats, supervise, shut down.
4. On T-UI, `fw::TastySession::tick` steps its `Stage` enum: hide the OSD, map / draw / show / wait / hide the splash, load the core, wait for the core to identify itself, start, run, wait out the linger time, load the menu core again, done. A `TastySession::Run` object (`PlayRun` or `RecordOnlyRun`) says whether this run loads a core and replays a movie or only records. It writes a JSON status file as it goes (`TastyStatusFile`).
5. `app::ReplayFeeder` steps its own stages (`IReplayStage::Stage`: Scanning, Hashing, Settling, Arming, Loading, Streaming, Stopping). It parses the movie through the codec for its format, compares the ROM's digest with the one in the movie header, applies the core settings the movie needs, sends an `Arm` message, asks for the ROM to be loaded, then streams `Input` messages and a final `End` through `ReplayRing` (a 256-slot `SpscRing` of `ReplayMsg`).
6. On T-RT, `app::ReplayGate` receives those messages. After the power-on event (end of the ROM download, or a reset pulse, as the core's `IReplayCore::power_on` says) it counts core frames, decides which counted frame is movie frame 0 (the epoch, by `app::EpochRule`), and from then on writes each `Input` record's pad masks to the core when its movie frame is due and the configured phase into the frame has passed. It publishes counters (`ReplayStatus`: on time, late, lost, delayed, gaps) that the session prints at the end.
7. When the movie ends, is stopped, or the gate disarms itself (`ReplayEnd`), the session lingers, loads the menu core, the process exits, and `/media/fat/MiSTer` runs again.

pages.title: Overview
pages.purpose: Introduce MiSTer Tasty for someone who has never seen it: what a TAS movie is, what `tasty` does on a DE10-Nano, what a user sees during a run (the menu goes away, a splash, the core boots, the run plays, the menu comes back), which systems and movie formats it handles and how well today, and what else is in the repository (installer, menu script, catalogue, compare tool, static build, CI). End with a map of the wiki: using it, how it works, building and contributing. Include the licence and the credits as the README gives them.

page_notes.content:
Source: `README.md` from the top through 'What it plays', and 'Credits and licence'. Keep the README's own status wording ('early', 'experimental', 'not working yet'); do not upgrade it. Give the status table (system, core, movie formats, status) in full. Do not reproduce the long tables of individual runs here; link the page 'Supported Systems and Movie Requirements'.

State plainly: Tasty needs the FPGA to itself for a run and returns to the normal MiSTer menu afterwards; it never downloads ROMs; it is not affiliated with the MiSTer FPGA project.

pages.title: Installation and Updating
pages.purpose: Explain how to install Tasty on a MiSTer and keep it current: the one-line `install.sh` command, what it writes and where (`Scripts/Tasty.sh`, then `tasty/tasty` and `tasty/tas-catalog.tsv` under `/media/fat`), the checks it makes before replacing a file, running it again to update, the `test-tasty.sh` wrapper that installs and then plays one random run the user's ROMs allow, the manual route (the binary from the releases page), and the recommended kernel settings with the reason for each.

page_notes.content:
Sources: `install.sh`, `test-tasty.sh`, the `update`, `update_binary`, `update_script` and `install_download` functions of `scripts/Tasty.sh`, and README 'Try it'. Facts to get right: every download goes to a temporary name beside the destination and is renamed over it only after a check (first line and a marker for the script; the published `tasty.sha256` plus an ELF magic check for the binary; a header row and at least one data row for the catalogue), so a failed download leaves the old file in place. Downloads are HTTPS only. The scripts touch only `Scripts/Tasty.sh` and the `tasty/` directory.

Kernel settings (README 'Recommended kernel settings'): `vm.compact_unevictable_allowed=0` and `vm.compaction_proactiveness=0` stop memory compaction from moving the locked pages of the real-time thread; the writeback workqueue's `cpumask` set to `1` keeps file writeback off CPU 1. Give the measured stalls the README cites and how to undo each setting. Mention that `scripts/Tasty.sh` applies the same three values for the length of a run it starts and puts the old values back (`tune_for_play`, `tune_restore`).

List the testing overrides (`TASTY_ROOT`, `TASTY_URL`, `TASTY_SHA_URL`, `TASTY_CATALOG_URL`, `TASTY_SCRIPT_URL`, `TASTY_ALLOW_FILE`) in a short table marked 'for testing', taken from the script headers.

pages.title: The Tasty Menu Script
pages.purpose: Document `scripts/Tasty.sh`, the entry a user picks under Scripts on the MiSTer: its sub-commands (`menu`, `scan`, `rescan`, `list`, `play <id>`, `stop`, `update`, `help`), the menu's sections (known-good runs, candidates, known to desync, not found, rescan, stop playback, update, quit), how it finds the user's own ROMs (by name under the platform's games folders, loose or inside zips, on the SD card, USB or a network share), how it confirms each by hash against the catalogue, the scan cache, how a movie is downloaded once and checked against its SHA-1, and how it finally calls `tasty play`.

page_notes.content:
Read the functions in order: `load_catalog`, `plat_dirs` / `plat_exts`, `game_roots`, `list_files`, `list_zip`, `name_match`, `rom_variants`, `rom_hashes`, the cache functions (`known_found`, `remember_found`, `prune_cache`), `scan`, `ensure_movie`, `check_args`, `play_row`, `cmd_menu`. Explain `rom_variants` with the catalogue's `layout` column: the hash is taken over the bytes the movie's emulator hashed (for example an iNES file without its header), which is why the same ROM can match under several layouts.

Say what is deliberately limited: a zip is opened only when its name holds the game's title; play options taken from a catalogue row are checked against an allow-list (`check_args`); two copies of the script at once are not supported because they share the scan cache; 'Stop playback' is reached from a second run of the script because `tasty play` blocks the first.

The script is POSIX `sh` for the BusyBox shell on the MiSTer image. Its tests are `tests/menu/run.sh`; mention them and link the testing page.

pages.title: TAS Catalogue
pages.purpose: Describe `data/tas-catalog.tsv`, the list of runs the menu offers: the file format (tab-separated, `#` comment lines, one header row), every column (`id`, `platform`, `title`, `aliases`, `region`, `rom_name`, `hash_kind`, `rom_hash`, `layout`, `movie_page`, `movie_url`, `movie_sha1`, `core`, `play_args`, `status`, `note`), the meaning of each `status` value and which menu section it lands in, where movies come from, and how to add or change a row.

page_notes.content:
The comment block at the top of the file is the specification; quote its definitions of `verified`, `reported`, `untested` and `desync`, of `rom_hash` / `layout`, and of `movie_url` (a tasvideos.org download, or a raw file at a pinned commit; `#<member>` names a movie inside a zip). State the rule in its first line: no ROM link is ever listed. Show two or three real rows as examples, wrapped for reading.

Explain the relationship to the README tables: the README's 'Known-good runs', 'Candidates' and 'Known to desync' are the human-readable view of the same runs. A user can add private rows in `catalog.local.tsv` beside the installed catalogue (`LOCALCAT` in `scripts/Tasty.sh`), which `load_catalog` reads after the shipped file.

pages.title: Command-Line Reference
pages.purpose: Give the complete `tasty` command line: the verbs (`play`, `info`, `check`, `status`, `stop`, `rec start`, `rec stop`, `help`), every playback option and every recording option with its argument, default and limits, the messages printed when an argument is refused, exit behaviour, and worked examples: play a movie with an explicit ROM, let tasty find the ROM, check a ROM first, record a run to AVI with the hash log, record only hashes, stop a run from a second shell.

page_notes.content:
Sources: README 'Command line' (the two option tables and the recording paragraphs) and, for exact spelling and limits, `tasty_print_usage` and the option table in `src/firmware/tasty_cli.cpp`, the `TastyRefusal::Why` values in `tasty_cli_refusal.h`, and `TastyRefusal::sentence_for` in `tasty_sentences.cpp`. List the refusal sentences next to the option they belong to. Give the process exit codes from `tasty::Exit::Code` in `tasty_exit.h`. Note option interactions the code enforces: recording options need `--record`; `--from` / `--to` only with `tasty play --record`; `--loop` not with `--record`; `--save` only with `play`; `check` needs `--rom`.

Explain the two kinds of invocation: `play` (and `rec start` with nothing running) becomes the long-lived owner process; `status`, `stop`, `rec stop` and a `rec start` that joins a running owner are short clients (the command classes in `tasty_command.cpp`, `TastyClient`). Name the files they use: `/tmp/tasty.lock`, `/tmp/tasty.pid`, `/tmp/tasty.status` (`src/firmware/tasty_paths.h`). A second `play` while one is running is refused with the busy text (`TastyPidFile::busy_text`).

Recording facts from the README to keep: recordings are the core's own pixels at native resolution in plain AVI; `cscd` is the default codec and `zmbv` is lossless; destinations must be under `/media/`; recording is best effort and never slows the replay; an AVI always has the `*.frames.tsv` hash log beside it.

pages.title: Supported Systems and Movie Requirements
pages.purpose: Say exactly what Tasty can play and what a movie must look like: the per-system status table, the movie formats per system (`.fm2` and `.bk2` for NES, `.lsmv` and `.bk2` for SNES, `.gmv` and `.bk2` for Genesis / Mega Drive, `.bk2` for PlayStation), the known-good runs, the candidates list, the runs known to desync and how far each gets, the `--lead` defaults and when to change them, what a movie needs (power-on start, standard pads, a matching ROM, the recorded core settings, power-on RAM on the SNES), and why a movie made on an emulator can drift on a faithful core.

page_notes.content:
This page is the README's 'What it plays' section and its sub-sections, kept faithful. pages.title: Architecture
pages.purpose: Give the one-page picture of how `tasty` is built: a single static process on the ARM side that owns the FPGA for a run; a stack of layers from Linux wrappers up to the executable; a set of threads with fixed roles, one of which is real-time and is the only one that talks to the core; and lock-free channels between them. pages.title: Core Link Protocol
pages.purpose: Document how the ARM side talks to a running core. Transport: data words (a byte or a 16-bit word wide, `hal::Width`) exchanged through two FPGA manager registers with a strobe / acknowledge handshake and three chip selects (`hal::SpiBus`). On top of it, `src/l1_proto`: identifying the core, reading its config string and capabilities, the status word and its bit fields, sending files (ROM downloads) with a file index, serving block requests for mounted images, sending pad, keyboard and mouse state, the OSD channel, reading the core's frame counter, and the `LinkOp` / `LinkEvent` messages other threads use to ask T-RT for link work. Then `app::LinkSession`, which sequences a session with one core from identification to live.

page_notes.content:
Sources: `src/l0_hal/include/hal/spi_bus.h` (the `gpo` bit constants, `SpiBus`, `ChipSelect`, `transfer`, `block_write`, `post`), `link_port.h`, `core_identity.h`, `core_capabilities.h`; `src/l1_proto/include/proto/`: `uio_opcodes.h`, `fio_opcodes.h`, `osd_opcodes.h`, `conf_str.h`, `conf_str_caps.h`, `capability.h`, `core_session.h`, `session_params.h`, `status_word.h`, `status_register.h`, `bit_field.h`, `download_session.h`, `spi_fio_queue.h`, `fio_window.h`, `block_server.h`, `block_slots.h`, `sd_request.h`, `joystick_port.h`, `frame_pad_encoder.h`, `held_pad_encoder.h`, `ps2_keyboard.h`, `frame_counter_read.h`, `frame_count.h`, `link_op.h`, `link_event.h`, `link_router.h`, and the `spi_*_decoder.h` files; `src/l4_app/include/app/link_session.h`, `link_binder.h`, `link_tx_channel.h`, `link_op_dispatch.h`.

The file names say 'spi' and the classes say 'Spi', but on this board the link is not a hardware SPI controller: it is words written to and read from two general-purpose registers (`mailbox_gpo_offset`, `mailbox_gpi_offset` in the board row) with a strobe bit. Say so once, then use the code's names.

This protocol is defined by the cores, which are separate projects; this repository implements the host side. Describe opcodes and fields only as far as these headers define them, with the constant names from the source. Where the tree also declares register lanes over the lightweight bridge or AXI (`axi_*.h`, `lw_*.h`, `sys_block_decl.h`), present them as an alternative transport a core may advertise through its capabilities, and keep the section short.

Make the replay connection explicit: the two link operations a replay depends on are the pad write (`JoystickPort`, one mask per port) and the frame-counter read (`FrameCounterRead`, an 8-bit wrapping counter per its `kWrapMask`); both run on T-RT inside the round budget.

pages.purpose: Explain precisely how an input reaches the core on the right frame. The feeder side on T-UI: the stage sequence, what the `Arm` message carries (ports, ROM file index, lead, phase offset, frame period, line-0 time, power-on time, parity rule, power-on event), and how `Input` records are batched into the ring ahead of time. The gate side on T-RT: waiting for power-on, the frame reference (the core's frame counter read over the link, or vsync from T-FRAME), detecting a new frame edge, deciding the epoch, computing the current movie frame from frame count, epoch and lead, the due test with the phase offset, writing the masks, and the counters and end reasons it reports. Finish with what `--lead` and `--phase` change and how to read the end-of-run report.

page_notes.content:
Sources: `src/l4_app/include/app/replay_feeder.h`, `replay_stage.h`, `replay_play.h`, `replay_msg.h`, `replay_control.h`, `replay_status.h`, `replay_gate.h`, `epoch_rule.h`, `frame_reference.h`, `core_frame_counter.h`; `src/l4_app/src/replay_feeder.cpp`, `scan_stage.cpp`, `hash_stage.cpp`, `settle_stage.cpp`, `run_stage.cpp`, `replay_gate.cpp`; `src/l4_app/src/rt_main.cpp` (`replay_step_`, `frames_step_`, and `drain_`, which tells the gate about a download end or a reset pulse); `src/l3_cores/include/cores/i_replay_core.h` (`Raster`, `PowerOn`, `Parity`, `PowerOnEvent`, `LeadRange`).

Walk `ReplayGate::tick`, `sample_ref_`, `decide_epoch_` / `decide_silence_`, `due_`, `apply_` and `write_` in order, with `FrameReference` (counts frame edges from the wrapping counter or from vsync samples, and dates each edge) and `EpochRule` (the arithmetic that picks the epoch) beside them. Define the terms as the code uses them. Edge: the moment the frame reference is seen to advance. Epoch: the counted frame that is movie frame 0, chosen from the delay between the power-on event and the next edge using the core's period, line-0 and power-on times (`EpochRule::pick`); if the choice is ambiguous the gate ends the run with `EpochAmbiguous` rather than guess, and the feeder's run stage starts the attempt again up to `ReplayPlay::kEpochTries` times. Lead: a whole-frame shift of the movie against the core. Phase: how far into the frame, after the edge, the pad is written (default half a frame per the README). Movie frame: frames counted since the epoch, minus the lead.

Explain the report honestly: `on_time`, `late`, `lost`, `delayed`, `pre_epoch`, `skipped_edges`, `held_rounds`, `gap_max_us`, `depth_min`, `pad_drops` and the `ReplayEnd` / `EpochFail` values are diagnostics about whether the host kept time. A clean report does not prove the game stayed in sync; that depends on the core matching the emulator. Use the constant names from `replay_gate.h` (`kReplayBudget`, `kAliasFrames`, `kFloorBack`, `kSlipNs`, `kGapNs`) and `epoch_rule.h` (`kEndSlackNs`) with the values in those files; do not restate them from memory.

pages.title: Core Settings, Power-On RAM and Saves
pages.purpose: Document how Tasty puts the core in the state the movie was recorded from, and how it protects the user's own data. Settings: each replay core lists the status-word fields a movie needs (`IReplayCore::setting_needs`), the feeder sets them in memory for the run and the session prints one line per changed setting, or refuses under `--strict`. RAM: the NES `--ram-init` choice; on the SNES the recorder's power-on RAM described as a `RamImageRecipe` (flat fills or a pseudo-random sequence), expanded and offered to a core that accepts a RAM image. Saves: the run uses a separate save directory and starts empty unless `--save` seeds a copy. Also `direct_video`, `--vsync-adjust`, and the muting of live controllers.

page_notes.content:
Sources: `src/l3_cores/include/cores/i_replay_core.h` (`SettingNeed`, `SettingNeeds`, `RamFill`, `ram_fill_need`, `check_settings`, `power_on_ram`), `ram_image_recipe.h` and `src/l3_cores/src/ram_image.cpp` (`RamImageRecipe::Kind` None / Flat / Pcg32 / Lfsr, `expand`, `kRamImageAddon`), `snes_movie_codec.cpp`, `snes_lsmv_codec.cpp`, `snes_bk2_codec.cpp` (where the recipe is derived from the movie header), `src/l4_app/src/addon_send.cpp` and `settle_stage.cpp`, `src/l4_app/include/app/session_owner.h` (`arm_replay_ini`, `set_replay_save_root`), `src/firmware/tasty_paths.h` (`kTastySaveRoot` is `tasty/saves`) and `replay_mode.cpp` (where the run's owner applies it), `src/firmware/tasty_session.cpp` (`copy_seed_`, `print_settings_`, `direct_video_resolved_`).

Follow the README's 'What a movie needs' for the user-visible behaviour and wording: settings are changed in memory only and the saved settings are left alone; the stock SNES core does not yet accept a power-on RAM image, so tasty says so once and the game starts from the core's own fill; many movies do not depend on it. Keep the README's link to the proposed core change as the README gives it. PlayStation needs the same BIOS file as the movie (`MovieFacts::firmware`, `IReplayCore::companion`); that is a file, not a setting.

Saves: state the guarantee and the mechanism together. The user's files under `saves/` are never opened or written; during a run the session's save directory is `tasty/saves`, the game powers on with no save unless `--save <file>` copies one in first (limited in size by `TastySession::kSeedMax`).

Summarise them in one table (core kind, class, what it handles) so a reader can navigate, and say explicitly that Tasty's documented, tested use is movie replay on NES, SNES, Genesis / Mega Drive and PlayStation, with the status the README gives. pages.title: Capture and Recording Pipeline
pages.purpose: Explain how `--record` and `tasty rec` produce an AVI and a per-frame hash log without disturbing the replay: where frames come from (the core's picture as it is handed to the scaler, read from FPGA-shared memory), the three seats (T-CAPTURE copies, T-ENCODE hashes and compresses, T-RECWRITE writes), the channels between them, frame numbering against both the core frame counter and the movie frame, duplicate and missed frames, the CSCD and ZMBV encoders and the motion-search and scale governors, AVI segmentation, the `*.frames.tsv` sidecar, the destination rules, and the status the session reports.

State the design rule from the README in the first paragraph: recording is best effort and the replay never waits for it. Then show how the code keeps that promise: the recording seats have lower priority than T-RT and run on the other CPU; frames are lent through bounded channels; when the encoder falls behind, `--scale auto` halves the picture and says so, and past that a frame is repeated and counted (`dup_reason` in the sidecar). Explain the writeback warning: writing to a network share can stall the real-time CPU unless the writeback mask is set, which is why tasty checks it when a recording starts.

Give the sidecar columns from `SidecarWriter::kHeader` and cross-link 'Comparing Against an Emulator'. Give the README's `ffmpeg` example for converting a recording.

pages.title: Code Conventions
pages.purpose: Explain the conventions a reader needs to follow the C++: C++23 with no exceptions and no RTTI; errors as `Ex<T>` (`std::expected<T, Error>`) with an `Errc`, an error site and a detail word; `[[nodiscard]]` throughout; small named value types instead of bare integers; facts as `constexpr` tables checked by `static_assert` and `consteval` functions; interfaces (`I...` classes) instead of function pointers; non-owning references (`OptRef`, `std::span`, `std::string_view`) and move-only owners (`UniqueFd`); the seat annotations; the warning set; the formatting style; and the absence of comments.

page_notes.content:
Sources: `cmake/warnings.cmake` (the full flag list, `-fno-exceptions`, `-fno-rtti`, `-ftrivial-auto-var-init=zero`, `TASTY_WERROR`), `.clang-format`, `src/infra/include/infra/error.h`, `opt_ref.h`, `unique_fd.h`, `fixed_str.h`, `affine.h`, `indexed_array.h`, `counter.h`, `seat.h`, and a `types.h` from two or three layers. Show one short real example of each idiom with its file path: a function returning `Ex<...>` and its caller; a value type with named constructors and no implicit conversion; a table with its `static_assert`; an interface and its implementation; a class with a seat annotation.

Explain how refusals travel: a user-facing refusal is a small enum-backed type (`TastyRefusal`, `cores::MovieRefusal`, `app::PlayRefusal`) carried in an `Error`'s detail word and turned into a sentence at the edge (`TastyRefusal::sentence_for`, `tasty_movie_refusal_sentence`, `tasty_refusal_sentence`, all in `src/firmware/tasty_sentences.cpp`), and the process status is a `tasty::Exit`. Say plainly that source files have no comments by design, so names, types and assertion messages are the documentation; advise readers to start from the headers.
